messages.subject: Limiting observations from a fitted detection function when
messages.subject_clean: Limiting observations from a fitted detection function when
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I recently received the following question, which may be of interest to
the group, so I will post it along with my answer here.

"Is it possible in dsm in R to use the global detection function limited
to the observations for a specific strata? I found a post/response on
the distance list that has a solution in Distance to use the "table for
values" option to select the detection function for each sighting. Is it
possible to do the same in R?"

So, in general, how does one fit a detection function to all
observations but then fit a DSM to a subset (say, in a strata)?

This is relatively straight-forward. The easiest way of dealing with
this is to take the fitted ddf object (using Distance or mrds) and
remove the observations that you don't want. dsm only cares about the
$fitted element of the detection function so the following code should work

ddf.obj$fitted <- ddf.obj$fitted[index]

where index is a vector of the elements you want to keep.

I hope this is helpful to folks on this list.

cheers,
--dave

PS. This question is archived at
https://github.com/dill/dsm/wiki/iFAQ#limiting-observations-from-a-fitted-detection-function

--

messages.subject: Distance sampling workshops in 2014
messages.body_plain:
The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental
Modelling (CREEM) is hosting two linked workshops in the summer of 2014
in our purpose-built facilities at the University of St. Andrews,
Scotland. The aim of these workshops is to train participants in the
latest methods for design and analysis of distance sampling surveys,
including line and point transects. The workshops are taught by leading
researchers in the field, using industry-standard software.

The first workshop (19-22 August) will run at an introductory level, and
will focus on distance sampling methods, largely described in the
standard reference book "Introduction to Distance Sampling." The
workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and participants will
learn how to use the program "Distance." Participants will gain a solid
grounding in both survey design and methods of analysis for distance
sampling surveys.  Note that we have moved the 'automated survey design'
and 'incorporating covariates in detection function' from the advanced
workshop into the introductory workshop.

The advanced distance sampling workshop (25-28 August) will include
advanced treatment of:  analyses in which detectability on the transect
line is not assumed to be perfect (the so-called g(0) problem) and
spatial (or  density surface) modelling. We will also showcase a series
of new R packages we have developed for performing standard as well as
sophisticated analyses in R. The aim of this workshop is to bring
participants up to date with the latest developments in distance
sampling methods and software. It is also an opportunity for those
actively engaged in the design, analysis and execution of distance
sampling surveys to discuss common issues and problems, and set future
research directions. The workshop will be a combination of lectures and
computer sessions, with considerable time for discussion.

For all workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own data
sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses with their data.
Computer sessions take place in our modern computer classroom (attached
to the seminar room); participants can use our computers or bring their
own laptops.

Additional details regarding the workshop can be found at our website

http://www.ruwpa.st-and.ac.uk/distance.workshops/distance2014/workshop_overview.html

--

messages.subject: Estimating degrees of freedom for collision risk models
messages.subject_clean: Estimating degrees of freedom for collision risk models
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I am calculating estimates of the numbers of birds potentially colliding
with turbines for offshore wind farms, for which the underlying estimates of
bird density are derived from distance sampling analyses.

To calculate confidence limits for these estimates I need estimates for the
variance and degrees of freedom for both the sums  and products  of various
individual components, each with their own variance/degrees of freedom
estimates. For example, the total number of collisions for the whole year is
based upon summing estimates for individual months, whilst the calculation
of the number of collisions for an individual month includes multiplying an
estimate of the density of birds by an estimate of the proportion at rotor
height.

Before doing this I just want to make sure that my planned approach to
estimate degrees of freedom and variance when combining different components
was reasonable.

When combining estimates by multiplying them my  plan was assume that it is
cv2 estimates for individual components estimates that are additive
(following equation 3.5 on page 52 of Buckland et al. 2001) and estimate the
degrees of from based upon Satterthwaite's equation but following equation
3.75 on page 78 and substituting cv2 estimates for the variance estimates in
Satterthwaite's original equation.

Conversely, when combining estimates by addition or subtraction my plan was
to assume it is variance  (rather than cv2)  estimates for individual
components that are additive and still estimate the degrees of freedom upon
Satterthwaite's equation but, as in the original equation, use variance
estimates instead of cv2 estimates in equation 3.75.

Is that reasonable, or I am barking up the wrong tree.

Many thanks

Nigel

messages.subject_clean: Errors in MCDS analyses of aerial survey data
messages.body_plain:
Hello all,

I'm having some trouble with my MCDS analyses that I'm hoping someonecan
shed some light on.  I am analyzing the results of a 2-year aerial survey
project for where a survey was conducted each month for 2 years in the same
area. The main goal of this study is to estimate density by season within
years, for example "Spring 2011" (8 strata), to examine changes in density
of sea turtles.  I have successfully analyzed the dataset using CDS
analysis and am fully comfortable with it's function and my results. I fit
a pooled detection function to compensate for low sightings in some seasons
(winter/fall) and then estimated density by strata.  Using model selection
to select from all possible models, a hazard-rate model with no adjustments
was selected as the best fit model.

The next step in my analyses is to incorporate environmental factors
(observer, weather, glare, sea state) to determine if MCDS improves the
model of the detection function and thereby estimates of density. Here is
where I'm encountering problems. I have a few errors that I'm hoping
someone can provide some guidance on:

1) ** Warning: Estimation routine failed to converge as could not calculate
area under pdf in iteration   9. Using results from previous iteration. **
** Warning: convergence failure **

   - I received this error when beginning MCDS analyses. I first tested
   only the hazard-rate model with no adjustments using all possible covariate
   combinations. Is it a good idea to use the model selected from CDS? So far
   I have tried all possible covariate combinations using only this model and
   very little trouble there. On some of the more complicated models (3 or 4
   factors) I receive this error though. I'm not sure why the model is not
   converging. Any suggestions as to how to deal with this?

messages.subject: Re: Study design/analysis
messages.body_plain:
On 22/01/2014 15:15, Rumble, Mark A -FS wrote:
> > What is the effect on the estimate of an animal moving then being observed on another transect?
None at all if it is random animal movement.  See p32 of the
introduction to distance sampling book.  If however the animal is
flushed by the observer, and flees to the next transect, where it is
flushed again, then positive bias will result.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: Re: Estimating degrees of freedom for collision risk models
messages.subject_clean: Estimating degrees of freedom for collision risk models
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,
I received two very useful responses from Eric Rexstad  and Rachel Fewster
to my question off list. As I think others are likely to be in a similar
position I will report the key bits of their responses here:
######################################################################
>From Eric:
I'm travelling at the moment and don't have Buckland et al. (2001) readily
available, so I can't speak to the equation numbers you reference.
Nevertheless, your fundamental approach to variances of sums and products
are essentially appropriate.

Eric also provided the following really useful reference:

Powell, L. A. 2007. Approximating variance of demographic parameters using
the delta method: a reference for avian biologists. Condor 109:950-955.
#########################################################################
>From Rachel:
this is just a quick note to say that your plan sounds reasonable to me.
I'm away from the office for the next few weeks and can't check up on the
references you've given, but the "squared CVs add" rule for products, and
"variances add" for additions and subtractions, usually perform OK.  They
both assume that the components of the product / sum are statistically
independent.
Unless there is strong dependence between the components, they should be all
right.  You could try some simple simulations in R where you check out how
important the dependence is, e.g. something like the commands below.

## Create a matrix of 1000 12-month estimates: each row corresponds to a set
of 12 months est <- matrix(0, ncol=12, nrow=1000)

## Fill in the first column (January estimates) as Normal(mean=100, sd=10)
est[,1] <- rnorm(1000, 100, 10)

## Fill in the following months with mild correlation to the previous month:
for(m in 2:12) est[,m] <- rnorm(1000, 0.9*100 + 0.1*est[,m-1], 10)

## Have a look at what you get: e.g. correlation between January and
February:
cor(est[,1], est[,2])

## Find the true variance of the sums from Jan to Dec:
var(rowSums(est))

## Find the summed variances var(Jan) + var(Feb) + ... + var(Dec):
sum(apply(est, 2, var))

## Won't be right, but maybe not too bad.

######################################################################
Hope that's useful to people.

Best wishes

Nigel
